title: O Absalom, my son (2 Samuel 19:1)
hook: the king weeps for the son who rebelled: "would I had died for thee"
carry: would I had died for thee
tomorrow: The wise woman of Abel (2 Samuel 20:14–22)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shimei threw stones from the ridge, and David kept walking. Your line was let him curse. Did you let one insult go by? Today, the war with Absalom ends, and the news reaches his father. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

Before the battle, the king stands at the gate as his army marches out, and he gives his commanders one order, loud enough for every soldier to hear: deal gently, for my sake, with the young man, with Absalom. Then he waits. The fighting is in the forest of Ephraim, and the forest, the text says, devours more people than the sword. Then a watchman on the wall sees a runner. Then another. David has only one question for each of them, and it isn't about the battle. Is the young man Absalom safe?
screen: `DEAL GENTLY WITH THE YOUNG MAN.` → `THE FOREST OF EPHRAIM.` → `IS ABSALOM SAFE?`

segments.voice: He wasn't. Riding a mule under the thick branches of a great oak, Absalom's head caught fast in the tree, and the mule went on without him, leaving him hanging between heaven and earth. A soldier saw him and wouldn't touch him, because of the king's order. Joab, David's commander, didn't hesitate. Absalom died there, and they threw him into a pit in the forest and heaped stones over him. The second runner, a Cushite, finally answers the king's question in the gentlest words he can find: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. And David understands. The verse that follows is all grief. The king is shaken. He goes up to the room over the gate and weeps, and as he goes he says: O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! "would I had died for thee", O Absalom, my son, my son! Over Saul and Jonathan, David made a song, with images and a refrain. Here there is no song. Just a few broken words, and the cry keeps circling back to one of them: my son. This is the son who stole the people's hearts, who drove his father barefoot out of the city, who came after his life. David's grief has no conditions on it. He doesn't say, if only he hadn't rebelled. He doesn't weigh what Absalom deserved. He wishes he had died in his place. The story doesn't let the moment stay private, though. The army's victory turns to mourning, and soldiers slip back into the city like people ashamed after a defeat. Joab comes in and tells the king, bluntly, that he is shaming the men who saved his life. And David gets up and sits in the gate. Both things are in the text: a father's grief that holds nothing back, and a king who still has to face his people.
screen: `CAUGHT IN THE OAK.` · `THE RUNNER'S GENTLE NEWS.` · then, large: `WOULD I HAD DIED FOR THEE.` · then: `MY SON, MY SON.` · `THE KING SITS IN THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: grieve without conditions. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a loss you've told yourself you shouldn't feel so much: someone who chose to walk away, a friendship that ended by their doing, a family that never became what you hoped. Notice if your grief keeps adding a but. They chose it, but. I should be over it, but. For a few breaths, drop the but. Just let yourself miss what you miss, with nothing attached. If you pray, you can remember them before God by name. The bell holds the time.
O Absalom. A father's cry over the son who rebelled against him, my son, my son, wishing he had died instead. Today's word.
Your line: would I had died for thee. Today, think of one person you love whose story with you isn't simple, and love them without the but. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Jews read David's lament for Absalom as part of the book of Samuel; in Jewish Bibles the cry is the opening verse of chapter 19, while English Bibles that follow the King James numbering place it at the end of chapter 18.

original.note: Hebrew: my son Absalom, from David's cry in 2 Samuel 19:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: a father mourning a lost son.
what it means: David grieves without conditions for the son who drove him out and sought his life.
what a scholar hears: Jewish Bibles number this cry 19:1; the King James puts it at 18:33. same verse, different count.
